summary:
Oregon sits in the fifteen-jurisdiction "Most Protective" tier of a July 2026 national legal-risk ranking compiled from a rubric covering thousands of tracked anti-trans bills, among them youth care bans, bathroom bans, birth-certificate and driver's licence restrictions, and measures removing legal recognition. The rubric describes the laws in this tier as having gone beyond baseline safeguarding of trans rights.

Statewide anti-discrimination law covers the settings a visitor uses daily. The Oregon Equality Act, signed 9 May 2007 as Senate Bill 2 and in force since 1 January 2008, prohibits discrimination in employment, housing, public accommodation, public education and public services on the ground of gender identity. Sexual orientation is defined to include gender identity regardless of whether a person's identity, appearance, expression or behaviour differs from what is traditionally associated with sex assigned at birth. The protections apply uniformly across the state and do not depend on the locality; religious employers, organisations and institutions are exempt.

Bias-motivated violence carries enhanced penalties: state hate-crime statutes add punishment for crimes committed because of the victim's gender identity. SB704, passed and signed in May 2021 and effective 1 January 2022, abolishes the gay panic and trans panic defences in murder, manslaughter and hate-crime cases.

Identity documents are comparatively accessible. The driver-licensing agency has offered an X marker for neutral or non-binary identity on licences and state IDs since 1 July 2017, and X is also available on birth certificates. Sex reassignment surgery has not been required to change the gender marker on a birth certificate by request since 2014. Legislation in May 2017 abolished the 1991 requirement that transgender people publish their names in newspapers before a legal change of sex. A circuit court ruling on 10 June 2016 allowed a resident to change gender to non-binary, which the Transgender Law Center believed was the first ruling of its kind in the country. An October 2019 executive order added gender identity to a 1987 policy barring state agencies from unlawful discrimination and required a third gender option X; legislation signed in June 2021 updated the 2008 definition of gender identity.

Care is shielded for people arriving from states that have banned it. Oregon's shield law, signed by Governor Tina Kotek on 13 July 2023, protects patients and providers from civil or criminal charges or investigation when care that is legal in Oregon was prohibited in the patient's home state. The House passed the bill in May 2023; the Senate passed a version with amendments after a Republican boycott.

Partner recognition does not turn on the parties' birth sex. Federal district judge Michael McShane struck down the 2004 constitutional amendment banning marriage for same-sex couples on 19 May 2014, marriages of same-sex couples performed elsewhere have been recognised since 16 October 2013, and gender-neutral marriage was codified effective 1 January 2016. Domestic partnerships have been available since 4 February 2008.
tangentialFactors:
The July 2026 ranking assesses enacted legislation against a rubric; it does not measure enforcement or day-to-day treatment, so Oregon's placement reflects its statutes rather than documented policing practice. The same tier includes California, Washington and Minnesota.

Federal pressure on Oregon institutions is active. In June 2025 the U.S. Department of Education announced a Title IX investigation into the Oregon Department of Education over its allowance of transgender women competing in women's sports.
localsOnly:
Public coverage of gender-affirming care is established. A January 2013 discrimination settlement committed the state to full medical insurance coverage of gender-affirming surgeries, drugs and related treatment for people on public employee health plans, and in August 2014 officials announced that Medicaid would cover gender-affirming hormone therapy and other gender-affirming care.

Conversion therapy on minors has been banned since 1 July 2015, under a bill signed 18 May 2015 after House and Senate votes of 41-18 and 21-8; Oregon was the third state to enact such a ban.

Residents' records have been corrected by statute. Legislation signed 6 May 2019 amended a 1951 mental health law that equated transvestites with paedophilia, passing the House 58-2 and the Senate 29-0.

A transgender-inclusive public schools policy survived challenge: the district court ruled against the plaintiffs on 24 July 2018, the Ninth Circuit affirmed on 12 February 2020, and the Supreme Court denied certiorari in December 2020. The anti-bullying law covers harassment, including cyberbullying, in all public schools.

Adoption and family formation are open to same-sex couples, married or unmarried, who may apply to adopt; lesbian couples have access to assisted reproduction such as in vitro fertilisation, with the non-genetic, non-gestational mother recognised as legal parent if married; surrogacy is neither expressly prohibited nor permitted and courts are generally favourable. In July 2025 the Ninth Circuit held unconstitutional the state's requirement that prospective adopters respect, accept and support a child's gender expression and sexual orientation, after the Department of Human Services prevented a woman seeking to adopt.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Oregon-specific data was located on police stops, searches, custody treatment or airport screening of trans travellers, or on how the public-accommodations law is enforced in practice against venues that exclude trans patrons.

Hate-crime statutes provide enhanced penalties for gender-identity bias, but charging and prosecution statistics for such crimes in Oregon were not found in the sources.

The 2023 shield law reached the Senate in amended form after a Republican boycott; which categories of care remain covered by the narrowed text is unresolved in the sources.

The practical effect of the July 2025 adoption ruling on Department of Human Services practice is not yet documented.

Federal rules on passports, visa markers, entry screening and federal facilities apply in Oregon but belong to the national record and are not restated here.
